source.version: arXiv preprint 2607.26899 (retrieved from arxiv.org/pdf/2607.26899; the document shows no version number or posting date). Title page: 'This is a preprint of a manuscript that has not undergone peer review.' Writers recruited March 11-15, 2026; evaluators April 13, 2026.
source.title_on_document: Human diversity fuels collective creativity that large language models cannot simulate or sustain

supplement.where: SI Appendix, pp. 23-29 of this PDF. Data, materials, and code on OSF: https://osf.io/amgx9/overview?view_only=46c491afd0ba40fc91f361aa2b53be79 (p. 17).
supplement.holds: Tables S1-S3 (p. 28-29): mixed-model coefficients with 95% CIs and p-values for centroid similarity and divergent/convergent ratings; Fig. S1 (metaphor + explanation embeddings), Fig. S4 (quantile regressions), Fig. S9 (other preregistered diversity measures), Fig. S10 (LLM-based scoring), Figs. S5-S8 (AI system prompts). No standard errors are printed anywhere; coefficients come with 95% CIs.

paper_design_summary: 644 Prolific writers (318 native English, L1; 326 non-native, L2) each wrote four creative metaphors with a short explanation under one of three conditions: human-only, AI ideation (GPT-4o supplies five candidate metaphors with explanations), or AI refinement (writer writes own metaphor, GPT-4o supplies five candidate explanations); L2 writers in the AI conditions chose English or their native language for the AI interaction. Collective diversity was scored as each metaphor's embedding cosine similarity to the leave-one-out centroid of its condition-by-scenario pool, and 351 blinded evaluators rated novelty, surprise, appropriateness, and explanation quality. A non-preregistered extension simulated the writer pool with persona-prompted LLMs (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-27b) and compared simulated pools with human pools on the same diversity measure.

studies.label: Human metaphor-writing experiment (L1/L2 x no AI / AI ideation / AI refinement)

assignment.what_was_assigned: GenAI condition (human-only, AI ideation, AI refinement). Writer background (L1 vs L2) is a measured factor set by eligibility screening, not assigned. Among L2 writers in the AI conditions, language of AI interaction (English vs native) was chosen by the writer. Scenario order was randomized within writer.
assignment.quote: The writing task followed a 2 × 3 between-subjects design, crossing writer background (L1 vs. L2) with GenAI usage (human-only vs. AI ideation vs. AI refinement).
assignment.locator: p. 17, Materials and Methods, Writing task and materials; also p. 4-5 Introduction ('participants generated metaphors in one of three conditions'). The paper never states that condition was randomly assigned; the only 'randomized' wording refers to scenario order (p. 17) and evaluator item order (p. 16).
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 4 and p. 20, Preregistration and deviations: https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity (three writing conditions, L1/L2 comparison, collective and individual outcome families; language choice preregistered as exploratory; LLM simulations and quantile regressions not preregistered)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Writers produced metaphors and explanations on their own in English with no GenAI; tab-switch detection deterred outside AI use.

arms.name: AI ideation
arms.description: Before each metaphor, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) supplied five candidate metaphors with explanations; writers could adopt, adapt, ignore, or regenerate. L2 writers could interact in their native language and receive English translations.

arms.name: AI refinement
arms.description: Writers first composed their own metaphor, then GPT-4o supplied five candidate explanations; writers finalized the explanation. The metaphor stayed the writer's own. L2 writers could interact in their native language.

participants.exclusions: Sessions terminated after a second tab/window switch: 24 (human-only), 23 (AI ideation), 18 (AI refinement) (p. 17-18). The paper does not say whether these sessions are outside the 644 recruited writers. Mixed models list N writer = 644 and 2,493 metaphor observations (Tab. S1, p. 28), fewer than 644 x 4 = 2,576; the gap is not explained. Per-arm and per-cell writer counts are not reported. 84 of 228 L2 writers in the AI conditions chose native-language interaction (39% in ideation, 34% in refinement; p. 8, p. 18).
participants.who: Prolific workers; L1 writers had English as sole native language and were born and residing in a majority-English-speaking country (n = 318); L2 writers had another native language (n = 326; 34 native languages). Mean age 36.1, 49% women.
participants.country: Not stated by country; L1 writers born and residing in majority-English-speaking countries; L2 writers' countries not stated.
participants.quote: We preregistered a target of 600 writers, 100 per cell in the 2 × 3 design, and ultimately recruited 644 writers via Prolific between March 11 and 15, 2026.
participants.locator: p. 16, Materials and Methods, Participants (Writers); N writer = 644 in Tab. S1 and Tab. S2, p. 28-29

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), via scripted system prompts (SI Figs. S5-S8)
ai_tool.how_used: AI ideation arm: five AI-generated candidate metaphors with explanations per scenario, with regeneration allowed (ideas_supplied). AI refinement arm: writer's own metaphor first, then five AI-generated candidate explanations (refinement). L2 writers could interact in their native language and received English translations to edit.

task.description: Four scenarios (boring class, disgusting food or drink, worst movie or TV show, messiest room), presented in random order; for each, one creative metaphor in the format 'It feels like ___. This is because ___', with instructions to be novel and surprising and avoid cliches.
task.duration: Median completion time 20 minutes for the whole survey (p. 16).

outcomes.name: Collective diversity: centroid similarity of metaphor-only embeddings
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each metaphor's embedding (only the 'It feels like ___' text) to the leave-one-out centroid of all other metaphors for the same scenario in the same condition; higher = less diverse (sign reversed relative to diversity). Primary collective measure, chosen after registration among the preregistered measures (p. 20). In the AI refinement arm the embedded metaphor text was written before the AI supplied explanations. Coefficients are from a treatment-coded mixed model with reference levels L1 and human-only, so the condition main effects are simple effects for L1 writers (p. 19).

contrasts.reported: Similarity (higher = less diverse). Tab. S1 metaphor: AI ideation (vs No-AI) b = 0.036, 95% CI 0.017 – 0.056, p < 0.001 (L1 simple effect); AI ideation × L2 b = 0.015, 95% CI -0.013 – 0.043, p = 0.284. Text: 'vs. human-only: b = 0.036, p < 0.001'. Group means (text p. 7-8): No AI L1 vs L2 M = 0.421 vs. 0.398, Δ = 0.024, p = 0.003; AI ideation L1 vs L2 M = 0.457 vs. 0.451, Δ = 0.006, p = 0.481. Fig. 2A plots means ± SEM by condition and group.

diversity_detail.metric: Per-metaphor cosine similarity to the leave-one-out centroid of the condition-by-scenario pool (mean centroid similarity); higher = less diverse
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each metaphor against the centroid of all other metaphors for the same scenario in the same condition (pools formed within condition, not within condition-by-language group per the Methods text)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear mixed-effects model on per-metaphor centroid similarity with random intercepts for writer and scenario (statsmodels); 95% CIs and p-values in Tab. S1; Fig. 2 error bars ± SEM
diversity_detail.notes: Pool membership is defined by condition and scenario (p. 18-19), so L1 and L2 writers in the same condition share a centroid; Fig. 2A then splits per-metaphor scores by writer group.

outcomes.name: Divergent creativity rating (novelty + surprise)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 351 native-English Prolific evaluators, blind to condition and background, rated each metaphor with its explanation on 0-100 sliders; novelty and surprise averaged (Spearman-Brown r = 0.86). Each evaluator rated 24 metaphors. Treatment-coded mixed model with random intercepts for evaluator, writer, and scenario; condition main effects are L1 simple effects. Robustness: quantile regressions at τ = 0.1-0.9 on metaphor-level mean ratings within writer background (Fig. S4, p. 13).

contrasts.reported: Tab. S2 divergent: AI ideation (vs No-AI) b = 4.75, 95% CI 2.00 – 7.50, p < 0.001 (L1 simple effect); AI ideation × L2 b = -3.92, 95% CI -7.79 – -0.05, p = 0.047; intercept 53.41. Text: L1 b = 4.753, p < 0.001; L2 b = 0.834, p = 0.548. Quantile regressions: L1 β = +7.5, p < 0.001 at τ = 0.1 vs. β = +4.5, p = 0.003 at τ = 0.9; L2 significant only at τ ≤ 0.2.
contrasts.locator: p. 12 text; p. 11 Fig. 4A; p. 13 text; p. 25 Fig. S4; p. 28 Tab. S2

contrasts.reported: Tab. S2 divergent: AI refinement (vs No-AI) b = 2.93, 95% CI 0.15 – 5.71, p = 0.039 (L1 simple effect); AI refinement × L2 b = -3.14, 95% CI -7.13 – 0.86, p = 0.124. Text p. 12: L1 'divergent: b = 2.930, p = 0.039'; L2 'divergent: b = -3.138, p = 0.124' (printed value equals the Tab. S2 interaction term). Quantile: L1 β = +6.3, p = 0.002 at τ = 0.1 and β = +5.1, p = 0.007 at τ = 0.2.
contrasts.locator: p. 12 text; p. 13 text; p. 11 Fig. 4A; p. 25 Fig. S4; p. 28 Tab. S2

outcomes.name: Convergent creativity rating (appropriateness + explanation quality)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 351 blinded evaluators; appropriateness and explanation quality averaged (Spearman-Brown r = 0.87); 0-100 scale. Mixed model with random intercepts for evaluator, writer, scenario; condition main effects are L1 simple effects. Robustness: quantile regressions (Fig. S4).

contrasts.reported: Tab. S2 convergent: AI ideation (vs No-AI) b = 3.13, 95% CI 0.86 – 5.39, p = 0.007 (L1 simple effect); AI ideation × L2 b = 0.58, 95% CI -2.61 – 3.78, p = 0.720; intercept 63.65. Text: L1 b = 3.127, p = 0.007; L2 b = 3.711, p = 0.001.
contrasts.locator: p. 12 text; p. 11 Fig. 4B; p. 28 Tab. S2

contrasts.reported: Tab. S2 convergent: AI refinement (vs No-AI) b = 3.24, 95% CI 0.95 – 5.53, p = 0.006 (L1 simple effect); AI refinement × L2 b = -1.76, 95% CI -5.05 – 1.54, p = 0.296. Text p. 12: L1 'convergent: b = 3.241, p = 0.006'; L2 'convergent: b = -1.756, p = 0.296' (equals the interaction term) and later 'L2 writers' convergent advantage was no longer significant (b = 1.485, p = 0.219)'. Quantile: L1 significant at five of nine quantiles (τ = 0.2-0.7); L2 only at τ = 0.9 (β = +2.6, p = 0.048).
contrasts.locator: p. 12 text; p. 13 text; p. 11 Fig. 4B; p. 25 Fig. S4; p. 28 Tab. S2

outcomes.name: LLM-judge creativity score (Bradley-Terry calibrated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three LLM judges (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen3-8B) repeatedly ranked randomly sampled metaphors; Bradley-Terry scores, z within rater. Preregistered individual measure that the paper set aside because judges disagreed with each other and with humans (Spearman ρ with human panel 0.30-0.37) and favored LLM content (p. 20).

contrasts.reported: Fig. S10B: standardized mean score (mean ± SEM) higher under AI ideation than No AI for all three LLM judges and for the human panel. No numbers or tests printed.

Fig. S10B: GPT-4o mini and Qwen3-8B judges score AI refinement below No AI; caption: 'two of the three LLM judges (GPT-4o mini, Qwen3-8B) sharply over-reward AI-ideation metaphors and penalize AI-refinement, a condition that the human panel does not produce.'

studies.label: LLM persona simulation of the writer pool vs human pools

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing assigned to people. For every writer, a persona prompt built from their background questionnaire was run through GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3.5-27b on the same four scenarios; simulated pools compared with the human pools.
assignment.quote: These simulation analyses were not preregistered; we treat them as an adversarial extension and stacked every analytic choice in the simulation's favor.
assignment.locator: p. 9 Results; p. 19 Methods, LLM simulation of the writer pool

arms.name: Human pools (no AI, AI ideation, AI refinement)
Simulated pools
arms.description: Persona-prompted GPT-4o mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18), Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-27b at default temperature 1.0; variants with native-language generation for L2 personas and temperature sweeps 0.5-2.0 (Claude up to 1.0).

participants.who: No new participants; personas mirror the S1 writers' backgrounds.
participants.quote: For every writer in all three conditions, we constructed a persona prompt from their background questionnaire

ai_tool.how_used: Models generate metaphors as simulated writers; no human receives AI help in this contrast.

task.description: Same four metaphor scenarios in the same two-part format.

outcomes.name: Collective diversity of simulated vs human metaphor pools (centroid similarity)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same centroid-similarity measure as S1-O1; higher = less diverse. Fluency checks: format adherence, gibberish share (wordfreq), GPT-2 perplexity.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Simulated pools (each model, default temperature, English)
contrasts.reported: Similarity (higher = less diverse); 'each simulation vs. human with AI ideation: Claude Δ = 0.102, Qwen Δ = 0.111, GPT-4o mini Δ = 0.241, all p < 0.001'. Claude Sonnet 4.6 'recovered only 75.3% of the diversity of the human-only pool.'

Claude Sonnet 4.6 vs. human with AI ideation: M = 0.528 vs. 0.457, Δ = 0.071, p < 0.001. Native-language vs English-only GPT-4o mini: M = 0.606 vs. 0.698, Δ = -0.092, p < 0.001. Fig. S3: native-language gain for L2 personas Claude Δ = 0.05, Qwen Δ = 0.06, GPT-4o mini Δ = 0.20, all p < 0.001.
contrasts.locator: p. 10 text; p. 9-10 Fig. 3B; p. 24 Fig. S3

contrasts.reported: Diversity 'plateaued around 0.50, leaving a persistent gap of 0.04 to the least diverse human pool'; GPT-4o mini at temperature 2.0 passed the plateau with 14.3% gibberish words and format adherence below 75%.

diversity_detail.metric: Per-metaphor cosine similarity to leave-one-out centroid; higher = less diverse
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each metaphor against the centroid of the other metaphors for the same scenario in the same pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-sided permutation tests with 10,000 iterations for pool-level human vs simulated comparisons (p. 19-20)
diversity_detail.notes: Context evidence only: compares AI-generated output with human output.

company_involvement.description: Authors at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development; no company funding or staff stated. The authors used Claude for language editing and analysis code (p. 1).

eligibility.reason: S1 is a preregistered 2 × 3 between-subjects online experiment in which writers worked under no AI, AI ideation, or AI refinement, with 644 writers in the analysis (Tab. S1, p. 28) and outcomes scored on the output (embedding centroid similarity, blinded human ratings). The paper never states that the GenAI condition was randomly assigned (p. 16-17; 'randomized' refers only to scenario and evaluator item order), so criterion 1 is unclear pending the preregistration or OSF materials. If assignment was random, S1 is core. S2 (LLM persona simulation vs human pools) is ai_vs_human context.

one_line_finding: Relative to no AI, AI ideation raised metaphor centroid similarity (less collective diversity; b = 0.036, 95% CI 0.017–0.056, p < 0.001) while AI refinement did not (b = 0.007, p = 0.516), and AI ideation raised L1 writers' divergent ratings (b = 4.75, p < 0.001) but not L2 writers' (b = 0.834, p = 0.548) (Tab. S1–S2, p. 28; p. 12).
open_questions: Was the GenAI condition randomly assigned? The PDF does not say; check the preregistration (https://tinyurl.com/DiverseCreativity) or OSF materials.
Per-arm writer counts are not reported; only L1 = 318, L2 = 326, and 228 L2 writers in the two AI conditions.
Are the 65 tab-switch terminations (24 + 23 + 18) outside the 644 recruited writers? Why are there 2,493 metaphor observations rather than 2,576 (644 × 4)?

The headline diversity coefficients (b = 0.036, b = 0.007) are simple effects for L1 writers under treatment coding (p. 19), though the text on p. 7 presents them as the general effect of each workflow.

On p. 12 the L2 refinement effects printed as 'divergent: b = -3.138, p = 0.124; convergent: b = -1.756, p = 0.296' equal the Tab. S2 AI refinement × L2 interaction terms, not L2 simple effects; elsewhere on p. 12 the L2 refinement convergent effect is given as b = 1.485, p = 0.219.
notes: Whole PDF read (29 pages, SI on pp. 23-29). No SEs printed; coefficients come with 95% CIs. The AI tool in S1 is scripted GPT-4o suggestions, not open chat: ideation = ideas_supplied, refinement = refinement (study-level role field set to ideas_supplied for the arm closest to free chatbot use). L2 language of AI interaction was self-chosen, so language-group contrasts within AI arms are non-randomized. In the refinement arm the metaphor text (S1-O1's scored text) was written before AI input, though the condition included AI. Evaluators (N = 351) rated each metaphor with its explanation; 8,241 rating observations in Tab. S2.
